summary.text: Valence electrons are the electrons in an atom's outermost shell, and they can take part in forming a chemical bond if that shell is not closed.
An atom with a closed shell of valence electrons, matching a noble gas configuration, tends to be chemically inert.
The number of valence electrons governs an atom's bonding behavior, so elements with the same number are often grouped together in the periodic table.

facts.label: Alkali metals
facts.value: Each atom has only a single valence electron

facts.label: Octet rule
facts.value: Main-group atoms tend to react toward 8 valence electrons

facts.label: 18-electron rule
facts.value: Transition metals tend to react toward 18 valence electrons

facts.label: Helium exception
facts.value: Two valence electrons, yet chemically very inert

items.prompt: A metal in group 1 reacts far more readily than most metals. What about its atoms explains this?

options.label: They carry an almost empty inner shell
They hold their electrons more tightly than any other metal
They have one valence electron that is easily lost
They are the largest atoms of any element

items.explain: An alkali metal has a single valence electron, which is easily lost to leave a positive ion with a closed shell.

items.prompt: A lamp is filled with neon, which barely reacts with anything. What about its atoms explains this?

options.label: Its valence electrons form a closed shell
It has no valence electrons to give away
It has one valence electron too few for bonding
Its nucleus holds on to every electron it has

items.explain: An atom with a closed shell of valence electrons, as in a noble gas configuration, tends to be chemically inert.

items.prompt: An element sits in group 16 of the periodic table. How many valence electrons does it have?
items.explain: In groups 13 to 18, the units digit of the group number matches the number of valence electrons.

items.prompt: A nickel atom's 3d electrons are not in its outermost shell, yet they count among its valence electrons. Why?

options.label: They are the same electrons as the ones in its 4s subshell
They are held more loosely than every other electron in the atom
Every inner-shell electron counts for transition metals
Their energy is close to that of the 4s electrons

items.explain: For transition metals the incomplete (n−1)d subshell is part of the valence shell, and those orbitals are all at similar energies to the outer ones.

items.prompt: A valence electron soaks up energy from a photon and jumps to a shell farther out, but it stays with the atom. What is this called?

options.label: Ionization
Atomic excitation
Covalent sharing
Core capture

items.explain: An energy gain that makes the electron jump to an outer shell is atomic excitation; ionization is when the electron breaks free of the atom.

items.prompt: Two atoms form a single covalent bond. Where do the electrons in that bond come from?

options.label: Each atom gives one electron from its outermost shell, forming a shared pair
One atom gives both electrons, and the other atom gives none
Each atom gives up one of its innermost electrons to the pair
Both electrons come from the atoms' nuclei, not their shells

items.explain: In a single covalent bond, a shared pair forms with each atom contributing one valence electron.

paragraphs.heading: The outermost electrons
paragraphs.text: Valence electrons are the electrons in an atom's outermost shell. When that shell is not closed, they can take part in forming a chemical bond. For a main-group element, they are the electrons in the shell with the highest principal quantum number n, and a higher n means a shell lies farther from the nucleus. For a transition metal, a valence electron can also sit in an inner shell.

paragraphs.heading: Why they matter
paragraphs.text: These electrons decide much of how an element behaves in chemistry. They set its valence: whether it bonds with other elements at all, how readily, and with how many. The electrons that do this are the ones with the highest energy. So an element's reactivity depends heavily on how its electrons are arranged. An atom whose valence shell is closed, matching a noble gas, tends to be chemically inert.

paragraphs.heading: Counting them
paragraphs.text: The periodic table makes counting easy. In groups 1 to 12, the group number equals the number of valence electrons; in groups 13 to 18, the last digit of the group number does. Phosphorus has the arrangement 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³, so it has 5 valence electrons in 3s² 3p³, and its highest valence is 5, as in the molecule PF₅. Helium breaks the pattern: it has two valence electrons, but its shell is full, so it is very inert and usually sits with the noble gases in group 18.

paragraphs.heading: Gaining and losing
paragraphs.text: Atoms one or two electrons away from a closed shell are reactive. Those with one or two extra are highly reactive, since they need relatively little energy to lose them, and they become positive ions. Those one or two short tend to pick up the missing electrons and become negative ions, or to share electrons instead. A nonmetal atom can fill its valence shell either by sharing electrons with a neighbouring atom, called a covalent bond, or by removing electrons from another atom, called an ionic bond.

paragraphs.heading: The octet and 18-electron rules
paragraphs.text: As a general rule, main-group elements other than hydrogen and helium tend to react until they reach an s²p⁶ arrangement. This is the octet rule, since each bonded atom then has 8 valence electrons, counting shared ones. Transition metals show a similar tendency toward d¹⁰s²p⁶. That is the 18-electron rule, with 18 valence electrons on each bonded atom.

paragraphs.heading: Metals down the table
paragraphs.text: The alkali metals of group 1, such as sodium and potassium, are the most reactive kind of metal. Each atom has just one valence electron, which it loses easily to become a positive ion with a closed shell, like Na⁺. Magnesium, in group 2, is somewhat less reactive, because each atom must give up two electrons to reach Mg²⁺. Going down any column of metals, reactivity rises: heavier atoms have more shells, so their valence electrons sit farther from the nucleus and are held less tightly.

paragraphs.heading: Trading energy with light
paragraphs.text: Like the inner electrons, a valence electron can take in or give out energy as a photon. Gaining energy can make it jump to an outer shell, which is called atomic excitation. With enough energy it can break free of the atom entirely, which is ionization, leaving a positive ion. When it loses energy and a photon is emitted, it can drop to an inner shell that is not full.
